newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians give huge "Yes" to new constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerians give huge "Yes" to new constitution.

text.p: Algerians have voted overwhelmingly for President Liamine Zeroual's draft constitution banning Moslem guerrillas from seeking power, state radio and television reported on Friday.
They said provisional referendum returns from most of the country's 48 regions showed there would be a large "yes" vote.

State media said threats of violence by Moslem militants had not materialised. Official figures showed Algerians had turned out in large numbers to vote in defiance of the threats and calls by main opposition leaders for a boycott.

High "yes" returns were reported in a number of areas, including 95 percent in the western town of Mascra and more than 90 percent in the southeastern region of El Oued and the southwestern province of Saida, said state radio.
The Berber-dominated northeastern town of Tizi-Ouzou was one of the exceptions with nearly 63 percent of the voters opposing the draft constitution, the radio added.
The planned constitution says Arabic will be the only state language, angering Berber activists who want official recognition for their language as well.
The lowest turnouts were in Berber areas, where a Berber-dominated party had called for a boycott. Only a quarter of the electorate in Tizi-Ouzou voted.
Algerian television said Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour would meet journalists in Algiers at about 9.30 a.m (0830 GMT) on Friday to issue final voting figures.
Thousands of voters took to the streets in the eastern city of Constantine to celebrate the end of the violence-free vote.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Thursday. By early evening nearly three-quarters of Algeria's 16.4 million eligible voters had cast ballots, state radio said, quoting the Interior Ministry.

Residents in the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, said the army shelled mountains near the city on Wednesday night, apparently trying to pre-empt any buildup of Moslem guerrillas. Blida is a route for guerrillas seeking to carry out attacks around the capital.
Guerrillas threatened before the referendum that they would kill anyone voting.
The national turnout was 71.94 percent at about 6 p.m (1700 GMT) on Thursday, compared to 65.82 percent in last year's presidential election at the same time, official figures showed.
The government had been hoping for a big turnout to bolster its popularity.
Algiers-based diplomats and independent analysts expected more than 70 percent of the voters to back the constitutional reforms.
The new constitution would bar politicians from campaigning on the basis of the Moslem faith, the Arab or Berber languages, gender issues or regional differences.
Diplomats said the government deployed more than 300,000 soldiers and policemen to guard voters across the country, five times the size of France.
Police and paramilitary forces were seen patrolling Algiers streets under drizzling rain. Soldiers in combat gear manned roadblocks on main routes outside the capital, witnesses said.
More than 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since 1992 when the authorities annulled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
The Armed Islamic Group, or GIA -- most feared of the country's Moslem guerrilla movements -- warned people not to vote on Thursday, threatening to slit the throats of anyone who left home.
A smiling Zeroual, who cast his ballot at a polling station near the presidential palace in Algiers, vowed to respect the voters' decision on his proposed reforms.
"The Algerian people is sovereign. Its will would be respected," Zeroual, a former army general, told reporters after he voted amid tight security.
Diplomats said hopes for change flowered last year but withered when violence continued and people felt the hardship of economic reforms required by overseas creditors.
"A year after the presidential election, political deadlock is still total," secular opposition leader Said Saadi said on Wednesday. "Social poverty is worsening every day."

"Even before the results of the referendum are known, the conclusions on the future of democracy are far from being optimistic," the Algerian Liberte newspaper said in a comment blasting the government for its tight control on the media.
